column1: # Step 3 (03-spark-32): m1 and m2, and the two held rules this rung contradicts.
# Written from step03/CHECKLIST-4.2.md sections 2 and 6. Read that file for what
# each requirement claims in Spark's terms; this one is only how it is measured.
# The two overrides, and why they are here rather than resolved by dropping the
# hold.
# step02.tsv's header predicted this file: "The first one of those appears at
# the step that leaves 3.0.3, where held-m1-spark-303 becomes false on a correct
# tree; it is written in that step's file rather than resolved by dropping the
# hold here." This is that step, and these are those lines.
# Dropping `hold m01.tsv` would have been the easy resolution and the wrong one:
# it would take twelve other step-1 rules down with it -- the Scala suffix, the
# absent spark-xml, the shaded-guava bans, the pinned plugins, the reproducible
# build -- none of which this rung contradicts. So the hold stays whole and the
# two rules it gets wrong are restated.
# They are restated as a *range* rather than moved to 3.2.4, and the difference
# matters. As preconditions their job is "step 1 has not been undone" -- the pom
# is not back at 2.4.0 -- and a tree that has not bumped the version yet has not
# undone anything, it simply has not finished. Pinning them to 3.2.4 would make
# the standing rules fail on such a tree, and a failed standing rule voids the
# whole migrated family: a candidate who did every bit of m2's work and left the
# pom alone would score zero on m2 as well. That is the ladder punishing an
# unfinished step as though it were a sabotaged one. So the precondition spans
# the fence, and m1-spark-324 below is what is actually paid for landing on it.
# m1 -- the fence. Two reads, deliberately not the same read twice: the pom says
# what the build resolved and the probe says what the code actually ran in. A
# tree can get the first right and the second wrong (a stale jar, a runtime
# Spark on the submit classpath), and the step is about the engine, not the
# declaration. The legacy-hatch half of m1 is in cheats3.tsv, priced at zero.
# m2 -- the milestone. describe() picks its five statistics by default; the
# program prints them. Naming them is what the migration is, and the gate reads
# it three ways: the calls are gone (source and jar), an API that takes the list
# is called instead, and the list is really there as text.
# `(summary|agg)` rather than `summary`, because the property is "the statistics
# are named", not "you called summary()". Both classes are checked for having
# neither today: AnalyzeWaterInteractions4 uses select/union/filter throughout
# and PdbLigandDemo uses groupBy/count/sort, so `select` would have been green
# on the untouched tree and these two are not. `stddev` is the discriminating
# name of the five -- "min" and "max" appear as words in 9 and 11 files, but
# "stddev" appears as a *string literal* nowhere in the 230 sources, and
# bytecode.strconst reads literals. count/mean/min/max are left to the replay,
# which prints a different table for any other list.
# m3 and m4 were here and are not any more. They read the adaptive-execution
# and statistical-aggregate settings off the run, and item 4.3 measured both
# green on a tree that changed nothing: the replay's spark-submit is the
# verifier image's, spark is `provided`, and the image is 3.2.4 whatever the pom
# says. Two requirements that no candidate can fail were paying a do-nothing
# tree 0.14. The five rules now live in rung3.tsv as standing rules -- same
# facts, same counterexamples, priced as a void rather than as a share -- and
# the semantics they stood for are still graded, through the replay. rung3.tsv's
# header carries the measurement and the argument.
